summary:
Top Traders Unplugged Systematic Investor 319: Rob Carver and Niels discuss CTA myths, bond/fiscal views, execution and rebalancing practice, and the diversification and replication papers.
Conclusions: CTAs are too small to move markets; avoid selecting strategies on noisy backtests; fewer independent bets than markets; return-based CTA replication is flawed.

coverage.note: intro; CTAs too small to move markets (pet hate)
oil and cocoa CTA positioning; vol targeting reduces size when vol expands
short vs long term trend followers; one month is not evidence
Fed cut and bond selloff; Paul Tudor Jones fiscal view
JGB widow maker; Rob's counterargument on US debt
sentiment on bonds; Rob short Bunds; Oct 2024 CTA performance and trend barometer
daily data, delayed-fill test, intraday and gap risk
dynamic optimisation, buffer, options vs trend following
volatility risk premium, calls vs futures, combined skew
rebalancing and transaction costs
position inertia buffer, correlation window for instrument returns
exponential weighting, strategy-level correlation window
system monitoring; no performance-based strategy allocation
do not select strategies on backtests; error bars; Yavin article intro
Yavin factor argument, equal weights, CTA factors
effective bets, performance scaling with markets, 300 market debate
skew from factors, core-satellite allocation, non-linear diversification
New Found replication paper: three replication methods
random data testing, dispersion, 30 futures sufficient
replication savings and cost numbers
return-based regression window, lasso, in-sample critique
simple ETF alternative, tracking error, return-only replication flaw
manager selection options and skill; wrap-up
nothing actionable: outro

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: we're actually quite quite small players and even even with a bit of leverage which obviously we use, we're not really big enough to to move things in in in markets
claims.claim: CTAs are too small relative to market size to be the cause of big price moves such as oil volatility, because their AUM and leverage are limited, except possibly in illiquid speculative pockets.
claims.testable: partly - could be tested by comparing estimated CTA position sizes with market volume

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: And actually I suspect that oil hasn't been a very good market for CTAs this year
claims.claim: Oil was a poor market for CTAs in 2024 because trend models went long early, were disappointed, and are now roughly flat or slightly short after the price fell from 87 to 65.
claims.indicator: oil price trend (high $87 in April, $65, $72 recently)
claims.direction: trend followers flat/slightly short crude
claims.testable: partly - CTA oil P&L could be checked in index data

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you can sort of plausibly say if there'd been a really long smooth trend, which you'd expect CTAs to buy into with big positions because the trend is smooth, therefore volatility is low, therefore leverage should be high
claims.claim: Vol-targeted trend followers hold their largest positions in smooth, low-volatility trends, so a sharp reversal after such a trend is the case where CTA deleveraging could amplify a move.
claims.direction: large positions build in smooth trends
claims.conditions: matters only after a long smooth trend that sharply reverses; not the case in oil
claims.testable: partly - position estimates from vol-scaled signals are replicable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Well, in fact, we've sold about 90% of our cocoa into that rally because as you mentioned, when vol expands, we contract our position size
claims.claim: Volatility-targeted trend followers cut position size as volatility expands, so a big rally such as cocoa in 2024 is accompanied by CTA selling of position size, the opposite of the claim that CTAs pushed the price up.
claims.direction: position size falls when vol rises

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you would expect the correlation between short-term trend followers and long-term trend trend followers to be probably not zero or negative, but it wouldn't it's not going to be especially especially high
claims.claim: Short-term and long-term trend followers have moderately positive but not high correlation because they pick up trends at different time scales.
claims.indicator: return correlation of short-term vs long-term trend CTA indices
claims.testable: yes - compute correlation of short vs long lookback trend returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: a short-term trend follower will be whipsawed because the market's kind of moving up slowly but in a series of sort of jagged pipes spikes
claims.claim: Short-term trend followers do well when trends occur over short periods, which whipsaws long-term followers, while long-term followers do well in slow trends with jagged spikes that whipsaw short-term followers.
claims.direction: short-term trend wins in short bursts, long-term wins in slow drift
claims.conditions: depends on the time scale of the prevailing trend
claims.testable: partly - regime classification of trend scale needed

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if if I had somebody working for me and who came up with a backtest that was one month long, they'd be out the door
claims.claim: One month of results (August 2024 short-term CTAs beating long-term) is not evidence for choosing a trend horizon; backtests need many years and economic cycles to avoid picking up temporary events.
claims.testable: yes - sample-size and significance can be computed

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: it pretty much started when the Fed cut 50 basis points, and which as was actually probably more than most people would have expected
claims.claim: In autumn 2024 the bond selloff began when the Fed cut 50 bp, which led to higher long-term yields rather than lower, hurting trend followers' fixed-income positions.
claims.direction: long-end yields rose after a larger-than-expected cut

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: may start to vote with their feet and give a vote of no confidence, not so much to the candidate, but actually to the budget plans that either of them really stands for
claims.claim: Paul Tudor Jones expects a point where bond vigilantes reject US fiscal plans, a Minsky moment, and said he would own no fixed income and would short the back end.
claims.indicator: US long-end Treasury yields, deficit path
claims.direction: short long-end Treasuries
claims.conditions: requires loss of confidence in US budget path
claims.testable: no - timing of a loss-of-confidence event is not testable

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Right now, the US debt, according to this interview, is $35 trillion. But the income from tax receipts is only 5 trillion per year.
claims.claim: Paul Tudor Jones cites US debt of $35tn, tax receipts of about $5tn and a deficit of about $2tn a year, with a path toward 200% of GDP in 30 years, as the basis of his fiscal-risk argument.
claims.testable: partly - data are public but the inference is a projection

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: not that many strategies are able to profit from a long-term bear market in in bonds, but but trend following has actually proven that it can very recently
claims.claim: Trend following can profit from a sustained bond bear market, as it did in 2022, unlike most strategies.
claims.direction: short bonds when trend is down
claims.testable: yes - CTA bond P&L in 2022 is observable

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: And you know one of the the great widow maker trades last 30 years was was shorting Japanese government bonds.
claims.claim: Shorting Japanese government bonds on deficit and demographic arguments was a widow-maker trade for decades because prices kept rising and yields stayed near zero.
claims.direction: long JGBs for trend followers, fundamental shorts lost
claims.conditions: fundamental debt arguments can fail for decades in a country with its own currency

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Um and one of the nice things, of course, about being you know, being trend followers is we could ignore all of that.
claims.claim: Trend followers avoid widow-maker fundamental calls by following price, which let them stay long JGBs for about three years until a sharp gap down in February 2013 closed the position.
claims.direction: long JGBs while trend up; exit on gap down
claims.testable: yes - JGB trend history is testable

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there's no reason why the US as a country can't support quite a large federal debt
claims.claim: Rob Carver expects the US to behave like Japan rather than face a Minsky moment because it prints its own reserve currency and can carry larger debt.
claims.direction: no forced US bond collapse
claims.conditions: holds while the dollar remains the reserve currency and demand for US assets persists
claims.testable: no - a regime view, not a rule

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: one of the things that happens as you get an aging society is people do move more of their investments into fixed income
claims.claim: Ageing populations shift savings into fixed income, increasing bond demand and keeping yields lower for longer.
claims.direction: bond yields lower
claims.testable: partly - demographics and yield link is testable but confounded

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: People are so excited and and they want to essentially just buy fixed income because now they can get four or five percent
claims.claim: Investor sentiment in late 2024 was strongly in favour of buying fixed income at 4 to 5% yields, which is opposite to Paul Tudor Jones's bearish concern.
claims.direction: investors buying bonds for yield

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I am short bunds.
claims.claim: Rob Carver's trend model was short German Bunds in October 2024 with no other fixed-income position, in line with Paul Tudor Jones's direction though not the US.
claims.direction: short Bunds

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: My own trend barometer finished at 32 last night
claims.claim: Niels's trend barometer at 32 is on the weak side and suggests trend followers will lose money this month.
claims.direction: trend followers lose money when barometer is low
claims.conditions: barometer measures how favourable current conditions are to trend following
claims.testable: yes - barometer vs monthly CTA index return can be regressed

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: SocGen trend down almost 3% this month now down 71 basis points for the year.
claims.claim: In October 2024 trend followers were hurt mainly by fixed income and equity corrections and some currencies, while gold and silver were the only strong liquid markets; SocGen trend was down almost 3% for the month.
claims.indicator: SG Trend Index, SG CTA Index, BTOP50, S&P 500, MSCI World
claims.direction: gold and silver positive; bonds, equities, FX negative

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: a really good test to do when you're doing your backtest on daily data is to see what effect has if you delay your fills by one one business day or even by two business days
claims.claim: For slow trend following, test sensitivity by delaying fills by one or two days; if the Sharpe change is above about 0.01 the system is sensitive to delay and needs hourly data or slower trading, otherwise intraday moves and overnight gaps do not matter.
claims.indicator: Sharpe ratio change when fills are delayed 1-2 days
claims.conditions: slow trading systems; not high frequency

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if you're trading slowly enough, then moving one, you know, the last price in a whole series of prices by a by even a quite a large amount won't change the desired position that much
claims.claim: A slow system's desired position barely changes if the latest price moves, so intraday and overnight price movements between signal and execution can be ignored on average.
claims.conditions: trading slowly relative to daily price noise

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: This is the portfolio I'd ideally want to have if I didn't have trading costs.
claims.claim: Dynamic optimisation compares current positions with the zero-cost ideal portfolio and trades only when moving is worth the cost, sometimes not trading at all or trading in cheaper markets.
claims.indicator: current vs ideal portfolio, trading costs
claims.direction: trade only if benefit exceeds cost
claims.testable: yes - cost-aware rebalancing can be backtested

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: which is vol adjusted, then if it was less than 10%, I wouldn't bother trading
claims.claim: A simple buffer skips a trade if the position changes by less than 10% of a standard vol-adjusted position unit.
claims.direction: no trade inside buffer

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So, we can actually treat trend following, particularly short-term trend following, as a bit like buying an option without buying an option.
claims.claim: Trend following has a long-option-like payoff (gains when markets trend, small losses whipsawing in ranges), particularly at short horizons, without paying the explicit option premium.
claims.direction: long convexity

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: So, buying options consistently is a money-losing strategy.
claims.claim: Systematically buying options loses money because of the volatility risk premium: implied volatility exceeds realized volatility on average since investors pay for insurance and certainty.
claims.direction: short options earns, long options pays premium
claims.testable: yes - variance risk premium is well documented

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: as the price goes up the delta of the option goes up, which means you've effectively got more exposure to the market
claims.claim: A long call automatically pyramids as price rises because delta increases, mimicking trend followers' increasing exposure.
claims.direction: more exposure as price rises

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: if implied volatility is currently really low um and actually below my forecast for historical volatility, it may make sense to buy the call option
claims.claim: Choose between futures and options for a directional view by comparing implied vol with forecast vol: buy calls when implied is below forecast, use futures when implied is high.
claims.indicator: implied volatility vs forecast realized volatility
claims.direction: long call when implied cheap; long future when implied expensive

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the positive skew properties of trend following combined with the negative skew properties of auction selling
claims.claim: A combined futures-trend plus option-selling system would be net short volatility yet keep trend following's positive skew, with a higher Sharpe than futures-only trend following in theory.
claims.direction: long trend, short vol bias
claims.testable: partly - requires option data to test

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: The more transaction costs are are are higher, the more tolerance you're going to have from being away from the position that you want
claims.claim: With zero costs one should always rebalance; as transaction costs rise, the optimal tolerance for deviation from the target position widens.
claims.direction: wider no-trade band when costs higher

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: What I'm probably going to do is buy go long and buy more of bonds that are cheaper to trade
claims.claim: A portfolio-level cost-aware optimiser can express a required bond exposure through the cheapest-to-trade correlated market and leave expensive positions untouched.
claims.indicator: relative trading cost across correlated instruments
claims.direction: buy cheaper substitute

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: standard annual standard deviation target is about 25% and I pay about 1% in transaction costs
claims.claim: A retail trader with 25% risk target pays about 1% a year in costs (half commissions, half spreads); an institution would pay about 60 bp (50 bp spread, 10 bp commission).
claims.indicator: annual transaction cost 1% at 25% vol target

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in theory, you should actually, yes, have a a wider buffer if an instrument's more expensive and a smaller buffer if it's cheaper
claims.claim: In theory the position-inertia buffer should be wider for expensive instruments and narrower for cheap ones; the fixed 10% is a simplification that suits retail single-lot trades.
claims.indicator: position buffer width by instrument cost

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I actually use um roughly a 6-month window, and I do use an exponentially rolling method
claims.claim: For measuring current portfolio risk, estimate correlations between instrument returns with an exponentially weighted window of about 6 months, balancing responsiveness against noise.
claims.indicator: 6-month exponentially weighted correlation of instrument returns

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: correlations always move to dramatic levels when when there's a crisis
claims.claim: Correlations between instruments move to extreme levels in crises because of flight to safety and simultaneous deleveraging, so safe-haven bond correlations rise.
claims.direction: correlations rise

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it will gradually dissipate out of your returns rather than jumping in in one go
claims.claim: Exponential weighting avoids sharp jumps in estimated correlation when a spike leaves a fixed window, which matters most for short windows.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: And because it's more stable, I actually want to use as much data as possible, 10 years, you know.
claims.claim: Correlations between trading-strategy returns (e.g. trend on Bund vs trend on US 10y) are lower and more stable than between assets, so estimate them over 10 or more years covering more than one cycle; exponential weighting matters little with that window.
claims.testable: yes - compare strategy vs asset correlation stability

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: publishes a web page every 10 minutes
claims.claim: Automated monitoring: a status web page refreshed every 10 minutes shows whether processes are running, crashed or stale, plus nightly emails confirming normal operation.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: here are the positions that that the broker thinks you have. Here are the positions I think you have
claims.claim: Automated checks flag missing prices for several days, missing daily positions, and differences between broker and system positions (often from expired futures) so human supervision is minimal.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: I usually almost completely ignore the performance of of strategies and and instruments
claims.claim: Do not dynamically reallocate capital between strategies or instruments on past performance because with decades of backtest and 10 years live data, differences are rarely statistically significant; simple allocation works as well as sophisticated optimisation which overfits.
claims.conditions: slow trading systems; high-frequency strategies have enough data
claims.testable: yes - test performance-based reallocation out of sample

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: all of the error bars overlap
claims.claim: Ranking about 100 instruments by backtested trend performance looks like a clear winner-loser spread, but with error bars all overlap, so selecting instruments or strategies by backtest results is mostly fitting noise.
claims.indicator: backtest Sharpe with confidence intervals across ~100 instruments
claims.direction: do not drop instruments with poor backtests

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: just think of the cocoa example where for 15 years it made no money and the last 18 months it's made all the money in the world for trend followers
claims.claim: Cocoa made no money for trend followers for 15 years then made the most in 18 months, illustrating that an instrument's past record is a poor guide to its future contribution.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: mathematically you actually get less diversification because you end up with less idiosyncratic sort of stock risk
claims.claim: Yavin's argument: adding more assets (even equal weighted) removes idiosyncratic risk and increases exposure to the common factor (e.g. S&P 500), so diversification benefits diminish.
claims.indicator: portfolio factor exposure vs number of holdings
claims.testable: yes - factor regression as holdings increase

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in the absence of any information about stock performance you should have equal weights
claims.claim: Equal weights are preferable to market-cap weights in long-only portfolios absent performance information, because cap weighting bets on mega caps being worth 50 times the smallest; momentum makes cap weighting look better.
claims.direction: equal weight
claims.conditions: momentum raises weight of winners in cap-weighted portfolios

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: there are probably four, maybe five factors out there that that potentially explain CTA performance
claims.claim: CTA performance is driven by a handful of latent macro factors (e.g. commodity move, 2008 risk-off with stocks down and bonds up) that change over time.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: well actually you've got five bets
claims.claim: With 300 markets a trend portfolio really holds a few independent macro bets, so idiosyncratic markets like cocoa contribute little and macro trends drive performance.
claims.indicator: number of markets vs effective independent bets
claims.testable: yes - effective bet count via PCA

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the increase in performance in a back test of a trend following portfolio as I add markets to it it does increase by a factor of about four to five
claims.claim: Backtested trend performance rises about four to five times with more markets, implying roughly 16 to 25 independent bets of which only about half a dozen matter at any time.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: you're also adding the chance of 200 markets being stuck in a range and you losing money of those
claims.claim: Adding many markets also adds many chances of ranging markets, so more markets are different, not necessarily better.
claims.conditions: small position sizes in extra markets

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there is no evidence, in my opinion, that
claims.claim: Looking at performance databases, there is no evidence that CTAs trading 300 to 400 markets do better than those trading about 100 or fewer.
claims.indicator: CTA performance vs number of markets

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: for the best skew, you want as pure an exposure to those factors as possible
claims.claim: Positive skew in a large trend portfolio comes from exposure to underlying macro factors, since idiosyncratic left and right tails wash out, so purer factor exposure gives better skew.
claims.testable: yes - skew by number of markets

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: maybe people allocating to CTA should be thinking a little bit more like um people in in in stocks do, which is you have your kind of core beta allocation
claims.claim: Allocators could hold a vanilla low-cost CTA as core beta and add a lower-correlation CTA for alpha, as in equities.
claims.testable: partly - needs correlation and fee data

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the correlations potentially probably understate the amount of diversification that's available as you add more assets, especially in trend following
claims.claim: Because returns are non-linear, correlation understates diversification in trend following: benefits continue beyond where correlation analysis says they level off.
claims.testable: yes - compare realized vs correlation-implied gains

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: Position-level replication, which is where you start, you know you know what the positions need to be, and then you form a series of positions that get as close to that portfolio as you possibly can.
claims.claim: Three replication methods exist: position-level, bottom-up simple model, and return-based; position-level replication is fine and Rob uses it, trading about 20 instruments that replicate his 300-instrument portfolio.
claims.testable: yes - tracking error between replica and full portfolio

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: why don't I just build a really simple model that does that in, say, 30 liquid futures markets
claims.claim: Bottom-up replication builds a simple trend model on about 30 liquid futures: cheap and good for ETFs to reach investors who cannot meet minimums.
claims.indicator: simple trend model on 30 liquid futures

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: the return-based application is the one I have a problem with
claims.claim: Return-based replication, fitting positions to reproduce an index's returns, is the approach Rob objects to most.
claims.indicator: regression of CTA index returns on futures

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: rather than using real data, it uses random data, randomly generated data. And this is a brilliant approach that I think quants should use more um because it reduces the chances of overfitting
claims.claim: Testing replication on randomly generated pseudo-CTAs and a pseudo index avoids overfitting to the last 30 years of real trends and reproduces features such as yearly dispersion.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: in years with low dispersion, probably there were one or two big factors that, you know, everyone made their money out of.
claims.claim: Low CTA dispersion years indicate one or two dominant factors; high dispersion years indicate varied market events where different weights and trades lead to different results.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: you only need about, say, 30 futures as long as you choose your universe to have a reasonable amount of independence
claims.claim: In the simulated universe about 30 factors explain everything, so about 30 futures suffice if they are spread across asset classes and liquid; 30 US bond futures would not work.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: And then 275 basis points of unnetted transaction costs. And I'm kind of thinking compared to the cost we pay, compared to the cost you just mentioned, this seems high.
claims.claim: The paper's saving estimate of 200bp management fee, 110bp performance fee and 275bp unnetted costs looks too high; it implies a ceiling Sharpe near one for replication savings over tracking error.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it's probably not unreasonable to to be able to to make an extra 100, maybe 200 basis points through a combination of a little bit of transaction cost saving and a bit of a bit of fee saving
claims.claim: Realistic replication savings are about 100 to 200 bp (paper's actual BTOP50 result implied a 0.23 ratio, about 150bp), minus the replicator's own fees.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: What you're trying to capture here is the effect of what happens when people's position changes sign.
claims.claim: Return-based regression needs short windows to capture sign changes in CTA positions, but short windows with many futures regressors make regression infeasible, so the paper uses lasso.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: it still looks to me like they're doing an in-sample test
claims.claim: The replication paper's results appear in-sample; a proper test would refit weekly, hold positions the next week and measure tracking out of sample, which always does worse than in-sample.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: just do 30 futures in a very simple portfolio and just bung that into an ETF
claims.claim: A simple momentum model on 30 futures automatically captures sign changes and is a more sensible cheap trend product than regressing on a benchmark.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: But of course, managers are not trying to meet a benchmark. So I think the concept of tracking error as such is not so relevant.
claims.claim: Tracking error is not the right metric for CTA replication because managers do not target a benchmark; live replication products show lower than expected correlation to the benchmark on daily data.
claims.indicator: tracking error and correlation of replicators vs BTOP50/SG index

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: for me fundamentally it's not possible to to do a good replication job with a purely backward looking measure based only on returns
claims.claim: Return-only backward-looking replication cannot reproduce a CTA index's diversification, so marketing it as benchmark less fees is flawed.

claims.speaker: Rob Carver
claims.quote: well, actually, something like a bottom-up replication done cheaply may make sense to you
claims.claim: If investors believe a few risk factors drive CTAs and diversification across managers is limited, a cheap bottom-up ETF with about 30 markets at about 50bp is reasonable; return-based replication of an index of many managers is a bad move.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: because they must believe that within managers there is something called skill
claims.claim: Institutional allocators who select managers must believe in persistent manager skill, so settling for a replicator contradicts their role.
